docs.title: Federated Node - Documentation
docs.text: This documentation covers deploying, configuring, testing, and using the PHEMS Federated Node (FN).

docs.title: What is the Federated Node?
docs.text:
The Federated Node lets researchers run analytical tasks against sensitive datasets without the data ever leaving your institution. Analytics code (packaged as a Docker container) is sent to the data - not the other way around. Results are returned to the researcher after running locally inside your cluster.

It is built on the ICODA Common API standard and deploys as a Helm chart onto a Kubernetes cluster.

Core components bundled in the chart:

  • Flask/Python backend - the FN API
  • Keycloak - authentication and role-based access control
  • Traefik - reverse proxy and ingress (recommended for production)
  • PostgreSQL - FN metadata (users, datasets, tasks, audit logs) - you provide this externally

docs.title: Where to start
docs.text:
Understanding how it fits together: Architecture Overview covers the components, how Keycloak is wired in, the namespace and pod layout, and the database and firewall decisions you need to make yourself.

Deploying for the first time: Prerequisites, then your platform deploy guide, then Post-Deploy Testing.

Joining an existing federated network / outbound-only mode: The network operator will have told you to use the Task Controller. Complete your deployment first, then head to the Task Controller wiki.

Building an analytics container: Analytics Container Development covers the environment variables, base images, and output contract.

Giving a researcher access to run tasks: User Roles then Using the API for the dataset permissions call.

docs.title: Analytics Container Development
docs.text:
This guide covers everything you need to build a Docker container that runs as a task inside the Federated Node.

Your container receives database connection details, schema names, and any custom parameters as environment variables. It writes results to a known path on a mounted volume. That's the entire contract.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
Use the provided base images - they have the correct ODBC drivers pre-installed for all supported database engines:

Image Language ghcr.io/aridhia-open-source/python-base:0.0.1 Python ghcr.io/aridhia-open-source/r-base:0.0.1 R

Source: Federated-Node-Task-Base-Images

Example Dockerfile:

FROM ghcr.io/aridhia-open-source/python-base:0.0.1

COPY requirements.txt /app/
RUN pip install -r /app/requirements.txt

COPY analysis.py /app/

CMD ["python", "/app/analysis.py"]

docs.title: Environment variables
docs.text: The FN injects these environment variables into your container at runtime. You do not need to handle authentication or connection setup from scratch - use CONNECTION_STRING directly with your ODBC driver, or build a connection from the individual DB_* variables.

docs.title: Database connection
docs.text: Variable Description CONNECTION_STRING Pre-built ODBC connection string for the dataset's database engine. Use this with pyodbc or equivalent. See format details below. DB_HOST Database hostname DB_PORT Database port DB_NAME Database name DB_USER Database username DB_PSW Database password DB_SCHEMA Read schema (same as CDM_SCHEMA) DB_ARGS Any extra connection arguments configured on the dataset

docs.title: Schema
docs.text: Variable Description CDM_SCHEMA The read schema - the schema your queries should read from WRITE_SCHEMA The write schema - if your analysis writes results back to the database, use this schema ORACLE_SID The database name, provided separately for Oracle connections

docs.title: File datasets (DuckDB / SQLite)
docs.text: Variable Description DATASET_TYPE duckdb or sqlite DATASET_PATH Full path to the read-only database file, e.g. /mnt/dataset/clinic.duckdb

docs.title: Paths
docs.text: Variable Description INPUT_PATH Full path to the input file, if inputs was specified in the task definition and a pre-fetch was performed. Format: <mount>/<filename>.

docs.title: Custom parameters
docs.text:
Any key/value pairs passed in executors[0].env in the task submission body are injected as environment variables verbatim:

"executors": [
  {
    "image": "ghcr.io/your-org/your-analysis:1.0",
    "env": {
      "COHORT": "paediatric",
      "MIN_AGE": "0",
      "MAX_AGE": "18"
    }
  }
]

These become $COHORT, $MIN_AGE, $MAX_AGE in your container.

docs.title: CONNECTION_STRING format
docs.text:
The CONNECTION_STRING variable is an ODBC connection string. The exact format depends on the database engine configured on the dataset:

PostgreSQL: 

driver={PostgreSQL ANSI};Uid=<user>;Pwd=<password>;Server=<host>,<port>;Database=<name>;

Microsoft SQL Server: 

driver={ODBC Driver 18 for SQL Server};Uid=<user>;Pwd=<password>;Server=<host>,<port>;Database=<name>;

MySQL: 

driver={MySQL ODBC 9.3 ANSI Driver};Uid=<user>;Pwd=<password>;Server=<host>,<port>;Database=<name>;

MariaDB: 

driver={MariaDB ODBC 3.2 Driver};Uid=<user>;Pwd=<password>;Server=<host>,<port>;Database=<name>;

Oracle: 

driver={Oracle ODBC Driver};Uid=<user>;PSW=<password>;DBQ=<host>:<port>/<name>;

DuckDB (file dataset): 

driver={DuckDB Driver};Database=/mnt/dataset/<path>;access_mode=read_only;

SQLite (file dataset): 

driver={SQLite3};Database=file:/mnt/dataset/<path>?mode=ro&immutable=1;

For file datasets the file is also mounted read-only at DATASET_PATH (with DATASET_TYPE set to duckdb or sqlite), so you can open it with the native library instead of ODBC. DB_USER, DB_PSW, WRITE_SCHEMA and ORACLE_SID are not set. See Datasets.

Using it with pyodbc:

import os
import pyodbc

conn = pyodbc.connect(os.environ["CONNECTION_STRING"])
cursor = conn.cursor()
cursor.execute(f"SELECT * FROM {os.environ['CDM_SCHEMA']}.patients LIMIT 10")
rows = cursor.fetchall()

docs.title: Writing results
docs.text:
Write all output files to /mnt/data (the default task_pod_results_path). The FN zips the contents of this directory and returns it to the researcher.

import os

output_dir = "/mnt/data"
os.makedirs(output_dir, exist_ok=True)

results_df.to_csv(f"{output_dir}/results.csv", index=False)
fig.savefig(f"{output_dir}/plot.png")

If the task was submitted with a custom outputs mapping, your container will have named subfolders mounted at the paths you specified. For example, with:

"outputs": {
  "figures": "/app/output/figures",
  "tables": "/app/output/tables"
}

Write to /app/output/figures and /app/output/tables - those paths are backed by the FN's persistent volume and will be included in the results archive.

If no outputs are specified in the task submission, a default results folder is created at the task_pod_results_path (/mnt/data by default) and anything written there is collected.

docs.title: Pre-fetched input data (db_query)
docs.text:
If the task is submitted with a db_query field, the FN runs a pre-fetch step before your container starts. A separate init container executes the SQL query against the dataset database and writes the results as a CSV file to the input mount path. Your container then receives the CSV rather than connecting to the database directly.

This is useful for analytics images that don't have database drivers installed, or where you want to separate the data extraction step from the analysis.

The pre-fetched CSV is available at $INPUT_PATH (full path including filename). Example:

import os
import pandas as pd

df = pd.read_csv(os.environ["INPUT_PATH"])

The db_query task submission field:

"db_query": {
  "query": "SELECT patient_id, age, diagnosis FROM public.patients WHERE age < 18",
  "dialect": "postgres"
}

dialect should match the source database engine (postgres, mssql, mysql, oracle, mariadb). db_query is not available for DuckDB/SQLite file datasets - the task reads the file directly. The pre-fetch connector translates the query if the source and target dialects differ.

docs.title: Resource limits
docs.text:
By default the FN does not enforce resource limits on task pods. You can request specific CPU and memory in the task submission:

"resources": {
  "requests": {
    "cpu": "500m",
    "memory": "512Mi"
  },
  "limits": {
    "cpu": "2",
    "memory": "4Gi"
  }
}

CPU values accept millicores (500m, 1, 0.5). Memory values accept Kubernetes units (128Mi, 2Gi, 512M). Limits must be greater than or equal to requests.

docs.title: Container requirements
docs.text:
The FN's pod security context runs all containers as non-root (runAsNonRoot: true, UID 1000) with all Linux capabilities dropped. Your container image must be compatible with this:

  • Do not require root for your entrypoint or runtime
  • Do not use USER root as the final USER instruction in your Dockerfile
  • Avoid operations that require elevated privileges at runtime

The base images provided already comply with this.

docs.title: Registering your image
docs.text:
Before the FN will run your container, you need to:

  1. Push the image to a container registry
  2. Register that registry with the FN (see Using the API)
  3. If federatedNode.enable_image_whitelist: true is set, also add the specific image to the FN allowlist
# Register the registry
curl --location "$FN_HOST/registries/" \
    --header 'Content-Type: application/json' \
    --header "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
    --data '{
        "url": "ghcr.io/your-org",
        "username": "your-github-username",
        "password": "your-github-PAT"
    }'

# Allowlist the image (only needed if enable_image_whitelist: true)
curl --location "$FN_HOST/containers" \
    --header 'Content-Type: application/json' \
    --header "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
    --data '{
        "name": "your-analysis",
        "registry": "ghcr.io/your-org",
        "tag": "1.0"
    }'

docs.title: Minimal working example
docs.text:
A complete Python analysis container that reads from the database and writes results:

import os
import pyodbc
import pandas as pd

conn = pyodbc.connect(os.environ["CONNECTION_STRING"])

schema = os.environ["CDM_SCHEMA"]
cohort = os.environ.get("COHORT", "all")

query = f"""
    SELECT age, diagnosis, COUNT(*) as count
    FROM {schema}.patients
    WHERE cohort = ?
    GROUP BY age, diagnosis
"""

df = pd.read_sql(query, conn, params=[cohort])

output_dir = "/mnt/data"
os.makedirs(output_dir, exist_ok=True)
df.to_csv(f"{output_dir}/summary.csv", index=False)

print(f"Done. {len(df)} rows written to {output_dir}/summary.csv")

With Dockerfile:

FROM ghcr.io/aridhia-open-source/python-base:0.0.1

RUN pip install pandas

COPY analysis.py /app/

CMD ["python", "/app/analysis.py"]

And the task submission:

curl --location "$FN_HOST/tasks/" \
    --header 'Content-Type: application/json' \
    --header "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
    --data '{
        "name": "cohort-summary",
        "executors": [
            {
                "image": "ghcr.io/your-org/cohort-summary:1.0",
                "env": {
                    "COHORT": "paediatric"
                }
            }
        ],
        "tags": {
            "dataset_id": 1
        },
        "description": "Age and diagnosis summary for paediatric cohort"
    }'

docs.title: Architecture Overview
docs.text:
This page explains how the Federated Node (FN) is put together: what each component does, how they talk to each other, which pods land in which namespace, and the design decisions you need to make yourself before going to production.

If you just want to install it, start at Prerequisites and Deploy: Core. Come back here when you need to explain the system to a security reviewer, or when you are deciding where to put the database and how to lock down the network.

docs.title: The idea in one paragraph
docs.text: The FN inverts the usual data sharing model. Instead of copying patient data out to a researcher, the researcher sends their analysis code to you, packaged as a Docker image. The FN runs that image inside your cluster, against your data, in an isolated pod that lives only as long as the task. The only thing that leaves is the result files, and only after they have been produced. Everything else stays behind your firewall.

docs.title: The components
docs.text:
Everything below is deployed by a single Helm chart. Some parts are subcharts you can turn on or off.

Component What it is What it does Backend Flask/Python application The FN API itself. Handles authentication checks, dataset registration, task submission, result retrieval, and audit logging. It is also the thing that creates task pods, so it holds Kubernetes API permissions. Keycloak Customised Keycloak deployment Identity and access management. Issues tokens, stores users, and holds the per-dataset permission model. See the Keycloak section below. Keycloak realm initialiser Small controller run at install time Waits for Keycloak to come up, loads the FN realm configuration, and creates the first admin user if you configured one. PostgreSQL Your own instance, or an in-cluster one for development Two logical databases. One holds FN metadata, the other holds Keycloak's own tables. Traefik Subchart, optional but recommended Reverse proxy and ingress. Terminates TLS and routes traffic to the backend and to Keycloak, using Gateway API HTTPRoutes. cert-manager Subchart, optional Issues and renews TLS certificates if you are not bringing your own. Result cleaner CronJob Deletes completed task pods, their volumes, and their results after cleanupTime days. Task Controller Subchart, only in outbound mode Watches a GitHub repository for task submissions and calls the FN API from inside the cluster, so the node never needs to accept inbound connections. There is a section on it below.

A couple of small helper containers do supporting work rather than running as long-lived pods. One prepares the databases and storage directories before the backend starts. Another runs inside each task pod, ahead of the researcher's own container, to pull data out of the registered dataset and drop it on the shared volume.

docs.title: How the pieces connect
docs.text:
A researcher reaches the node over HTTPS, through Traefik. Traefik routes them either to Keycloak, to log in and collect a token, or to the backend, for everything else.

The backend sits in the middle and talks to four things. It calls Keycloak to check that a token is valid and that the user is allowed to do what they are asking. It reads and writes its own PostgreSQL database for datasets, tasks, users and audit records. It calls the Kubernetes API to create task pods, secrets and volumes. And it reads finished results off the shared results volume.

The task pod itself talks to your research database to collect its input, and writes its output to the shared volume. Nothing else.

A few things worth calling out because they surprise people:

  • The backend writes to Keycloak, it does not just read from it. Registering a dataset or granting someone access to one creates records in Keycloak. This is why the backend needs Keycloak administrative credentials rather than just a client secret.
  • The backend talks to Keycloak over plain HTTP inside the cluster, at http://keycloak.<keycloak-namespace>.svc.cluster.local. TLS is terminated at the ingress. If your security policy requires encryption in transit inside the cluster, that is a service mesh job and is not something the chart does for you.
  • Task pods do not talk to the backend. They read their inputs from a mounted volume and write results to the same volume. The backend polls pod status. This keeps the analysis container as dumb and as unprivileged as possible.
  • The task pod never gets a Kubernetes service account with any rights. The credentials it does get are the database connection string for the dataset it was granted, injected as an environment variable.

docs.title: What Keycloak is doing here
docs.text: Keycloak does more in the FN than the usual "log in and hand out a token". It is the place where all access control decisions are made and stored, and the backend defers to it rather than keeping its own permission tables.

docs.title: Logging in and identity
docs.text: All FN users live in a single Keycloak realm created by the chart. A researcher authenticates against Keycloak directly and receives a token, which they then present to the FN API on every call. The FN never sees or stores a user's password. Adding, removing, and disabling users is Keycloak's job.

docs.title: Deciding who can do what
docs.text:
Access control works on two levels.

The coarse level is roles. There are four, running from a super administrator with full control of the node, through an administrator who manages datasets and tasks, to a standard researcher who can only do what they have been explicitly granted, plus an internal role used for service to service calls. User roles sets out what each one can call.

The fine level is per dataset. A researcher may be allowed to run tasks against one dataset but have no visibility of another, and roles alone cannot express that. So each registered dataset is represented inside Keycloak as its own protected object, with a set of actions attached to it such as viewing the dataset, running a task against it, or administering it. Granting someone access creates a rule in Keycloak linking that user to that dataset and those actions.

When a request arrives, the backend asks Keycloak whether this token is permitted this action on this dataset, and acts on the answer. The decision is Keycloak's, not the FN's.

The practical consequence is worth remembering: your access control configuration lives in Keycloak, not in the FN database. Backing up one and not the other leaves you with a node that knows about its datasets but has lost every user and every permission grant.

docs.title: Acting on a user's behalf
docs.text: Keycloak is also configured to let the backend obtain a token on behalf of a user, so that work can continue for a researcher when their session is not live. This is deliberate and necessary, but it does mean that whoever holds the Keycloak administrative credentials can effectively act as any user on the node. Treat those credentials as the most sensitive secret in the deployment.

docs.title: Where Keycloak keeps its data
docs.text: Keycloak uses the same PostgreSQL server as the FN but its own separate database, created at install time if it does not already exist.

docs.title: Namespaces and pods
docs.text: The chart spreads itself over several namespaces on purpose, so you can apply different network and admission policies to each. All names are configurable under namespaces in your values file.

docs.title: Release namespace (whatever you install into, for example federated-node)
docs.text: Pod / object Kind Notes backend Deployment The FN API. Three init containers run first: create the FN database if missing, run Alembic migrations, and create the results directory on the shared volume. db Deployment Only present if create_db_deployment: true. Development convenience, not for production. result-cleaner CronJob Removes expired tasks and results. backend-configmap, backend-secrets ConfigMap, Secret Backend configuration and credentials. Results PersistentVolume and Claim PV / PVC The shared results storage. Dataset credential secrets Secret One per registered dataset, holding the username and password for that research database. Copied into the tasks namespace as well.

docs.title: keycloak namespace
docs.text: Pod / object Kind Notes keycloak StatefulSet Keycloak itself, listening on port 8080 inside the cluster. Defaults to 2 replicas. keycloak-realm-init Deployment The realm initialiser. It stays running but is idle after setup. keycloak-config, kc-secrets ConfigMap, Secret Keycloak configuration and the admin password. Copied database secret Secret The chart copies your database secret here at install time, since Keycloak needs it too.

docs.title: tasks namespace
docs.text:
This namespace holds nothing at rest. It is where analysis pods are created, run, and deleted.

Pod / object Kind Notes Task pods Pod One per submitted task. Named after the task. Has an init container that fetches data from the registered dataset, then the researcher's own container. Result fetch jobs Job Created on demand when someone calls /results. Zips the task's output folder so the backend can read it. Per-task PVCs PVC Scratch space for the task, deleted by the cleaner. Dataset credential secrets Secret Copies of the dataset secrets, so task pods can mount them.

docs.title: fn-controller namespace
docs.text:
Only created when outboundMode: true.

Pod / object Kind Notes analytics-operator Deployment The Task Controller. A single replica, deliberately, since it is a stateful watcher of a git repository. Two init containers run first: one prepares its working directory, the other creates its own service user in Keycloak. analytics custom resource CRD Installed by the subchart. Each submitted task becomes one of these objects. Controller PersistentVolume and Claim PV / PVC Its git working area. This is separate storage from the results volume and needs sizing in its own right. controller-config ConfigMap Where the backend and Keycloak live inside the cluster, plus storage and task settings. controller-delivery-config ConfigMap The delivery destinations that results are pushed back to. controller-user-creds Secret The controller's own Keycloak service account credentials, generated at install time.

docs.title: fn-certmanager namespace
docs.text: Only created when the cert-manager subchart is enabled. Holds cert-manager and its issuers.

docs.title: The lifecycle of a task
docs.text:
Putting it together, here is what happens when a researcher submits a task.

  1. The researcher gets a token from Keycloak using their username and password, or uses a long lived token issued earlier.
  2. They POST /tasks with the image name, the dataset, and any input query.
  3. The backend validates the token against Keycloak and asks it whether that user is allowed to run tasks against that dataset.
  4. If image allow-listing is enabled, the backend checks the requested image exists in one of the registered container registries. It authenticates to the registry using stored credentials and checks the tag or digest.
  5. The backend creates a PVC and a pod in the tasks namespace.
  6. The backend records the task in its database and writes an audit entry.
  7. When the researcher calls /results, the backend creates a job that mounts both the task volume and the shared results volume, zips the output, and the backend streams the archive back.
  8. After cleanupTime days, the cleaner CronJob deletes the pod, the volume, and the stored results.

If task review is enabled (see Task review), step 7 requires a human approval first.

docs.title: The Task Controller and outbound mode
docs.text: Everything above assumes researchers can reach your node over HTTPS. Many hospitals cannot allow that. Outbound mode, enabled with outboundMode: true, removes the inbound path entirely: the node opens connections out, and nothing needs to be exposed to the internet.

docs.title: How it changes the flow
docs.text:
In outbound mode the researcher never calls your API. Instead they open a pull request against a GitHub repository that the network operator has set up. The Task Controller, running inside your cluster, watches that repository. When it sees a submission it clones the repository into its own working area, turns the submission into a Kubernetes custom resource, and then calls the FN API from inside the cluster on the researcher's behalf. From the backend's point of view nothing is unusual: it receives an ordinary task request over the cluster network and creates a task pod exactly as it always would.

When the task finishes, the controller collects the results and pushes them back to the destination configured for it, normally the same GitHub repository. The researcher picks them up there.

So the submission path and the results path both run outbound, over HTTPS, to a single endpoint you control.

docs.title: What it adds to the deployment
docs.text:
• A custom resource type. The subchart installs an analytics CRD. Every task submission becomes one of these objects, holding the image to run, the dataset requested, the submitting user, the source repository, and any inputs, outputs and environment variables. This is useful operationally: you can list them with kubectl to see what has been submitted, independently of the FN's own database.
  • Its own persistent storage. The controller keeps a git working area on a volume, separate from the results volume. Configure it under fn-task-controller.storage.
  • Its own Keycloak service user. An init container creates a user in Keycloak for the controller, with a password generated at install time. This is the identity the controller uses when it calls the FN API, and it is why the controller counts as a service to service caller rather than as a person.
  • GitHub as an identity provider in Keycloak. If you configure fn-task-controller.idp.github, a post-install job registers GitHub as an identity provider in the FN realm. This is what lets the node tie a pull request to a real FN user, so the normal per-dataset permission checks still apply to a task that arrived via git. If you set controller.skipUserAuth, that mapping is skipped and submissions are not attributed to a user at all, which is only appropriate for a closed test setup.
  • Broader cluster permissions. The controller's service account is bound to its own role over the custom resources, and, when it runs as part of the FN chart, to the backend's role as well. Treat it as being as privileged as the backend.

docs.title: What it means for your network and security review
docs.text:
• Nothing inbound. You do not need a public endpoint, a load balancer, or a certificate for the API. This is usually the entire reason for choosing outbound mode.
  • Outbound to GitHub becomes a required path. The controller polls GitHub continuously and pushes results back there. If you run an egress allowlist, GitHub has to be on it, and you should scope it as tightly as your proxy allows. This is a real data egress route and should be reviewed as one, not treated as ordinary internet access.
  • The GitHub repository becomes part of your access control. Whoever can open a pull request against that repository can put a task in front of your node. The FN still applies its own dataset permission checks on top, so a submission from someone with no grant on a dataset will be rejected, but the repository permissions are now the outer gate. Confirm who administers it and who can merge.
  • Results land somewhere you do not control. Once the controller pushes results back to GitHub, they are outside your firewall. If that matters, enable task review so a person approves the output before it leaves.
  • Keycloak still matters just as much. Outbound mode does not remove Keycloak or bypass it. It just changes who calls the API.

Setup is documented in Outbound connection only mode.

docs.title: Storage
docs.text:
The FN needs a ReadWriteMany volume shared between the backend and the result jobs. The supported backends are Azure Files, AWS EFS, GCS, NFS, and a local host path for single node development. This choice is made at install time via storage in your values file and is awkward to change later, since it involves recreating PVs.

Size it for concurrent task output, not total data volume, since results are deleted after cleanupTime days.

docs.title: Open points to consider
docs.text: These are the decisions the chart does not make for you. Work through them before a production deployment.

docs.title: Databases
docs.text:
• Where does the FN's PostgreSQL live? The chart can deploy one in-cluster with create_db_deployment: true, but this is meant for development and has no backup story. For production, use a managed instance or a properly administered one on your own infrastructure.
  • Is the connection encrypted? Set db.enforceSSL: true to make the FN connect with sslmode=require. It is off by default. Turn it on unless the database is on the same host.
  • Back up Keycloak's database as well as the FN's. They are separate databases on the same server. Restoring only fndb gives you a node that knows about its datasets but has lost every user and every permission grant.
  • Your research databases are entirely your problem. The FN stores a hostname, port, schema, and a credential secret per dataset. It supports PostgreSQL, MSSQL, MySQL, MariaDB and Oracle. Decide what account the FN connects with. It should be a dedicated, read-only account scoped to exactly the schema you intend to expose, not an application or admin account.
  • Where does the research database sit relative to the cluster? Task pods connect to it directly. If it is outside the cluster, that path needs to be open, and that has firewall implications covered below.

docs.title: Network and firewall
docs.text:
• Inbound. In the standard mode, researchers reach the FN over HTTPS, which means one public or VPN-reachable endpoint fronted by Traefik. Both the API and the Keycloak login endpoint need to be reachable, since the researcher authenticates directly against Keycloak. If you cannot accept inbound connections at all, use outbound connection only mode, where nothing needs to be exposed.
  • Outbound: container images. The cluster must be able to pull the FN's own images from their public registry, and it must be able to pull whatever analysis image a task requests. If your cluster has no internet egress, you need to mirror both into an internal registry. The backend also makes outbound HTTPS calls to registry APIs to check that an image exists before creating a pod.
  • Outbound: results delivery. If you enable the delivery API or the Task Controller, the cluster makes outbound calls to GitHub or another endpoint you configure. That is a deliberate data egress path and should be reviewed as one. See the Task Controller section above for what outbound mode changes.
  • Network policies are not shipped with the chart. There are no NetworkPolicy objects in the templates. If you want to stop a task pod from reaching the internet, or from reaching anything other than the one database it was granted, you have to write those policies yourself.
  • Segmentation between namespaces. The tasks namespace is where untrusted code runs. Treat it accordingly, and consider whether it should be allowed to reach the release namespace or the Keycloak namespace at all. It does not need to.

docs.title: Trust in analysis containers
docs.text:
The FN runs container images supplied by researchers. Nothing in the platform inspects what that code does. The controls available to you are:

  • federatedNode.enable_image_whitelist, which restricts task images to registries you have registered with the node.
  • Task review, which puts a human approval step between task completion and results leaving the node.
  • Network policy, as above.

Decide which of these you need. A node that will accept tasks from an open federation needs all three. A node used by a known internal team may not.

docs.title: Secrets and credentials
docs.text:
• Use pre-created Kubernetes secrets referenced from your values file rather than embedding credentials in the values file. The chart supports this throughout.
  • The Keycloak admin password is the crown jewel, because anyone holding it can obtain a token as any user on the node. If you do not set firstUserSecret, it is auto-generated and stored in the kc-secrets secret. Rotate it and store it somewhere sensible.
  • Kubernetes secrets are base64 encoded, not encrypted, unless you have enabled encryption at rest on etcd or are using an external secrets provider. Check which is true for your cluster.

docs.title: Upgrades
docs.text:
• Database migrations run automatically as a backend init container on every deploy. This means a rollback of the Helm release does not roll back the schema. Take a database snapshot before upgrading across a minor version.
  • The Gateway API and Traefik CRDs are installed by you, not by the chart, so they are also upgraded by you. See Prerequisites.

docs.title: Where to go next

docs.title: Datasets
docs.text:
A dataset tells the Federated Node where a research database lives and how a task should connect to it. The FN stores the connection details and per-dataset permissions - it never copies or centralises the data.

There are two kinds of dataset:

  • Server datasets - a database server the task connects to over the network: PostgreSQL, Microsoft SQL Server, MySQL, MariaDB or Oracle. The FN keeps the credentials in a Kubernetes secret.
  • File datasets - an embedded database file (DuckDB or SQLite) sitting on a volume. The file is mounted read-only into the task pod. There is no server, host or credentials.

Registering, updating and deleting datasets needs the can_admin_dataset permission (Administrator or above). See User roles.

docs.title: Supported engines
docs.text:
type Kind ODBC driver used in CONNECTION_STRING Minimum FN version postgres (default) Server PostgreSQL ANSI any mssql Server ODBC Driver 18 for SQL Server any mysql Server MySQL ODBC 9.3 ANSI Driver any mariadb Server MariaDB ODBC 3.2 Driver any oracle Server Oracle ODBC Driver any duckdb File DuckDB Driver v1.21.0 sqlite File SQLite3 v1.21.0

DuckDB and SQLite need v1.21.0 or later. Older releases reject "type": "duckdb" with DB type duckdb is not supported. Upgrade the Helm chart to 1.21.0+ before following the file datasets section. The upgrade runs a database migration that adds the volume_claim and path columns to the datasets table.

The analytics container needs the matching ODBC driver installed. The FN task base images (Python and R) include all of them.

docs.title: Dataset fields
docs.text:
Field Server datasets File datasets Description name required required Unique name. Lower-cased on save. For server datasets this is also the database name used in the connection string. type optional required Engine, from the table above. Defaults to postgres. host required not allowed Database hostname port recommended not allowed Database port. Defaults to 5432 for every server engine, so always set it for anything other than PostgreSQL. username required on create not allowed Stored in a Kubernetes secret, never in the FN database password required on create not allowed Stored in a Kubernetes secret, never in the FN database schema optional optional Read schema, passed to tasks as CDM_SCHEMA. Defaults to main for file datasets. schema_write optional not allowed Write schema, passed to tasks as WRITE_SCHEMA extra_connection_args optional optional Appended to the end of the ODBC connection string, e.g. Encrypt=yes;TrustServerCertificate=no; volume_claim not allowed required Name of a PVC in the tasks namespace that holds the file path not allowed required Path to the file, relative to the root of the volume. Must not start with / or contain .. repository optional optional Link to a GitHub repository for outbound mode. Only one dataset can be linked to a given repository. catalogue optional optional Object with title, description and optional version dictionaries optional optional List of objects with table_name, field_name, description and optional label

The examples below assume $FN_HOST and an admin $TOKEN are set, as in Using the API.

docs.title: Server datasets
docs.text: Every server engine uses the same request shape - only type, port and any extra_connection_args change.

docs.title: PostgreSQL
docs.text:
curl --location "$FN_HOST/datasets/" \
    --header 'Content-Type: application/json' \
    --header "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
    --data '{
        "name": "omop_cdm",
        "type": "postgres",
        "host": "postgres.your-institution.example.com",
        "port": 5432,
        "username": "fn_reader",
        "password": "db_password",
        "schema": "cdm",
        "schema_write": "results",
        "extra_connection_args": "sslmode=require;"
    }'

docs.title: Microsoft SQL Server
docs.text:
curl --location "$FN_HOST/datasets/" \
    --header 'Content-Type: application/json' \
    --header "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
    --data '{
        "name": "omop_cdm",
        "type": "mssql",
        "host": "mssql.your-institution.example.com",
        "port": 1433,
        "username": "fn_reader",
        "password": "db_password",
        "schema": "dbo",
        "extra_connection_args": "Encrypt=yes;TrustServerCertificate=no;"
    }'

ODBC Driver 18 encrypts by default and validates the server certificate. If the server uses a self-signed certificate, use TrustServerCertificate=yes; instead.

docs.title: MySQL
docs.text:
curl --location "$FN_HOST/datasets/" \
    --header 'Content-Type: application/json' \
    --header "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
    --data '{
        "name": "omop_cdm",
        "type": "mysql",
        "host": "mysql.your-institution.example.com",
        "port": 3306,
        "username": "fn_reader",
        "password": "db_password",
        "schema": "omop_cdm"
    }'

MySQL has no separate schema level - a schema is a database - so schema is usually the same as name.

docs.title: MariaDB
docs.text:
curl --location "$FN_HOST/datasets/" \
    --header 'Content-Type: application/json' \
    --header "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
    --data '{
        "name": "omop_cdm",
        "type": "mariadb",
        "host": "mariadb.your-institution.example.com",
        "port": 3306,
        "username": "fn_reader",
        "password": "db_password",
        "schema": "omop_cdm"
    }'

docs.title: Oracle
docs.text:
curl --location "$FN_HOST/datasets/" \
    --header 'Content-Type: application/json' \
    --header "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
    --data '{
        "name": "orclpdb1",
        "type": "oracle",
        "host": "oracle.your-institution.example.com",
        "port": 1521,
        "username": "fn_reader",
        "password": "db_password",
        "schema": "CDM"
    }'

For Oracle, name is the service name: the connection string uses DBQ=<host>:<port>/<name>, and the name is also passed to the task as ORACLE_SID.

docs.title: What happens on registration
docs.text:
• The connection details go into the FN database. The username and password go into a Kubernetes secret named <host>-<name>-creds, created in both the FN namespace and the tasks namespace.
  • A Keycloak resource and admin policy are created for the dataset, so access can be granted per user. See Architecture.
  • If DB liveness is enabled (the default), each task pod first checks the database is reachable before the analytics container starts.

The response contains the new dataset's id and URL:

{ "dataset_id": 1, "url": "https://<host>/datasets/omop_cdm" }

docs.title: File datasets (DuckDB and SQLite)
docs.text:
Requires FN v1.21.0 or later. If you are on an older release, upgrade the chart first - see Deploy: Core.

File datasets let you publish a single DuckDB or SQLite file without running a database server. The file lives on a volume, and every task against the dataset gets that volume mounted read-only at /mnt/dataset. Because the mount is read-only, any number of tasks can read the same file at once and no task can change it.

Setting one up has two steps: make the file available as a PVC in the tasks namespace, then register the dataset pointing at it.

docs.title: 1. Make the file available as a volume
docs.text:
The simplest way is the datasetVolumes Helm value. Each entry creates a static ReadOnlyMany PersistentVolume, plus a PVC with the same name in the tasks namespace. Set exactly one storage backend per entry.

datasetVolumes:
  - name: clinic-files          # PVC name - used as the dataset's volume_claim
    capacity: 10Gi              # optional, defaults to 10Gi
    mountOptions: []            # optional
    azure:
      shareName: datasets
      secretName: azure-storage-secret   # optional, this is the default
      secretNamespace: tasks             # optional

The other backends:

    # On-prem / single node, a directory on the node
    local:
      path: /data/datasets

    # AWS EFS
    aws:
      fileSystemId: fs-xxxxxxxx
      accessPointId: fsap-xxxxxxxx   # optional

    # GCP, a GCS bucket via GCS FUSE
    gcp:
      bucketName: my-datasets-bucket

    # NFS
    nfs:
      url: nfs.example.com
      path: /exports/datasets

Then upgrade the release, and check the PVC is Bound:

helm upgrade federatednode federated-node/federated-node -f values.yaml
kubectl get pvc clinic-files -n <tasks namespace>

You can also create the PVC yourself instead of using datasetVolumes. Any PVC in the tasks namespace works, as long as it supports ReadOnlyMany (or the task pods all land on one node).

Copy the database file onto the storage, e.g. upload clinic.duckdb to the root of the datasets Azure file share. The path you register is relative to the root of that volume.

docs.title: 2. Register the dataset
docs.text:
DuckDB:

curl --location "$FN_HOST/datasets/" \
    --header 'Content-Type: application/json' \
    --header "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
    --data '{
        "name": "clinic-duckdb",
        "type": "duckdb",
        "volume_claim": "clinic-files",
        "path": "clinic.duckdb"
    }'

SQLite is the same with "type": "sqlite" and a path to a .sqlite/.db file. Files in subfolders are fine, e.g. "path": "2026/clinic.duckdb".

host, port, username, password and schema_write are rejected for file datasets. schema defaults to main, which is the default schema in both DuckDB and SQLite. No Kubernetes secret is created.

When a task is submitted, the FN checks the PVC exists and fails the request with Volume claim <name> for dataset <dataset> not found if it doesn't, rather than leaving the pod stuck in Pending.

docs.title: What the task sees
docs.text:
Variable Example DATASET_TYPE duckdb DATASET_PATH /mnt/dataset/clinic.duckdb CDM_SCHEMA main CONNECTION_STRING driver={DuckDB Driver};Database=/mnt/dataset/clinic.duckdb;access_mode=read_only;

For SQLite, the connection string opens the file read-only and immutable:

driver={SQLite3};Database=file:/mnt/dataset/clinic.sqlite?mode=ro&immutable=1;

WRITE_SCHEMA, ORACLE_SID, DB_USER and DB_PSW are not set, and the DB liveness check is skipped since there is no server. Write results to the results folder, not to the database - see Analytics container development.

A task can use the ODBC connection string, or open the file directly with the native library:

import os
import duckdb

con = duckdb.connect(os.environ["DATASET_PATH"], read_only=True)
print(con.sql(f"SELECT count(*) FROM {os.environ['CDM_SCHEMA']}.person").fetchall())

library(DBI)
con <- dbConnect(duckdb::duckdb(), Sys.getenv("DATASET_PATH"), read_only = TRUE)

The db_query pre-fetch option is only available for server datasets. With a file dataset the task reads the file directly.

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
• The file is read-only. To publish new data, replace the file on the storage (or register a new path) - running tasks keep the file they opened.
  • Make sure the file isn't being written to while tasks read it. For DuckDB, close all writers and checkpoint the file before copying it into place.

docs.title: List and fetch
docs.text:
curl "$FN_HOST/datasets/" --header "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN"
curl "$FN_HOST/datasets/1" --header "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN"
curl "$FN_HOST/datasets/omop_cdm" --header "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN"

Credentials are never returned.

docs.title: Update
docs.text:
PATCH only the fields you want to change. Changing username or password updates the Kubernetes secret; changing host or name recreates it under the new name.

curl --request PATCH "$FN_HOST/datasets/1" \
    --header 'Content-Type: application/json' \
    --header "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
    --data '{
        "password": "rotated_password",
        "schema_write": "results_v2"
    }'

For a file dataset, point it at a new file:

curl --request PATCH "$FN_HOST/datasets/2" \
    --header 'Content-Type: application/json' \
    --header "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
    --data '{ "path": "clinic-2026-10.duckdb" }'

docs.title: Delete
docs.text:
Deletes the dataset record, its credentials secret, and any catalogue and dictionaries. For file datasets the PVC and the file are left alone.

curl --request DELETE "$FN_HOST/datasets/1" --header "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN"

docs.title: Catalogue and dictionaries
docs.text:
You can describe a dataset when you register it, so researchers know what's in it without seeing the data:

{
    "name": "omop_cdm",
    "...": "connection fields as above",
    "catalogue": {
        "title": "OMOP CDM extract",
        "description": "Inpatient episodes 2018-2025",
        "version": "5.4"
    },
    "dictionaries": [
        {
            "table_name": "person",
            "field_name": "year_of_birth",
            "label": "Year of birth",
            "description": "Patient year of birth"
        }
    ]
}

Read them back with:

curl "$FN_HOST/datasets/omop_cdm/catalogue" --header "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN"
curl "$FN_HOST/datasets/omop_cdm/dictionaries" --header "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN"
curl "$FN_HOST/datasets/omop_cdm/dictionaries/person" --header "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN"

docs.title: Granting access
docs.text: Researchers with the User role can't run tasks against a dataset until they're granted access to it. See Grant a user access to a dataset.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Error Cause DB type duckdb is not supported. FN is older than v1.21.0 - upgrade the chart host is required Server dataset registered without host username and password are required Server dataset created without credentials volume_claim, path not allowed for postgres datasets File fields sent with a server type (check type is set) host, port, ... not allowed for duckdb datasets Server fields sent for a file dataset path must be relative and can't contain '..' path starts with / or escapes the volume Volume claim <name> for dataset <dataset> not found The PVC doesn't exist in the tasks namespace Task pod waits on the DB liveness init container The server isn't reachable from the tasks namespace, or port is wrong (remember it defaults to 5432) Repository is already linked to another dataset PATCH the other dataset with "repository": null first

docs.title: Deploy: AWS (EKS)
docs.text: Work through Deploy: Core alongside this guide. The steps here are the AWS-specific additions to your values.yaml and any extra secrets to create.

docs.title: 1. Storage
docs.text:
The FN uses Amazon EFS (Elastic File System) to persist task results. The EFS file system must already exist before deploying.

You must also create an EFS Access Point - both fileSystemId and accessPointId are required fields. The access point ensures the FN pods mount with correct file permissions.

In the AWS console, when creating the access point set:

  • Root directory path: /files
  • Owner user ID: 1001
  • Owner group ID: 1001
  • Permissions: 777

See the AWS documentation on access points for full details.

docs.title: 2. TLS auto-renewal (optional)
docs.text:
If you want automatic SSL certificate renewal via AWS Route 53, create a secret with the required IAM role details. Values must be base64-encoded:

apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
metadata:
  name: aws-ssl-secret
  namespace: federated-node
data:
  EMAIL_CERT: <base64-encoded>
  REGION: <base64-encoded>
  ACCOUNT_ID: <base64-encoded>
  ROLE_NAME: <base64-encoded>
type: Opaque

docs.title: 3. Add the AWS block to values.yaml
docs.text:
Add this to your values.yaml (created in the core guide):

on_eks: true

storage:
  aws:
    fileSystemId: fs-xxxxxxxxxxxxxxx
    accessPointId: fsap-xxxxxxxxxxxxxxx

With TLS auto-renewal:

on_eks: true

storage:
  aws:
    fileSystemId: fs-xxxxxxxxxxxxxxx
    accessPointId: fsap-xxxxxxxxxxxxxxx

cert-manager:
  enabled: true

certs:
  aws: aws-ssl-secret

docs.title: 4. Deploy
docs.text: Return to Deploy: Core step 8 and run helm install with your completed values.yaml.

docs.text: Post-Deploy Testing

docs.title: Deploy: Azure (AKS)
docs.text: Work through Deploy: Core alongside this guide. The steps here are the Azure-specific additions to your values.yaml and the extra secrets to create beforehand.

docs.title: 1. Storage
docs.text:
The FN uses an Azure Storage Account file share to persist task results. The file share must already exist before deploying.

Create a Kubernetes secret with your storage account credentials:

kubectl create secret generic fn-azure-storage \
    --from-literal=azurestorageaccountkey="<your-storage-account-key>" \
    --from-literal=azurestorageaccountname="<your-storage-account-name>" \
    -n federated-node

Or via YAML (values must be base64-encoded):

apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
metadata:
  name: fn-azure-storage
  namespace: federated-node
data:
  azurestorageaccountkey: <base64-encoded-key>
  azurestorageaccountname: <base64-encoded-name>
type: Opaque

docs.title: 2. TLS auto-renewal (optional)
docs.text:
If you want automatic SSL certificate renewal via an Azure Service Principal, you need a secret and a ConfigMap.

Create the SP secret:

kubectl create secret generic fn-azure-ssl-sp \
    --from-literal=SP_SECRET="<your-service-principal-secret>" \
    -n federated-node

Create the ConfigMap with your Azure subscription details:

kind: ConfigMap
apiVersion: v1
metadata:
  name: fn-azure-ssl-config
  namespace: federated-node
data:
  EMAIL_CERT: admin@your-institution.example.com
  HOSTED_ZONE: your-institution.example.com
  RG_NAME: your-resource-group
  SP_ID: your-service-principal-app-id
  SUBSCRIPTION_ID: your-subscription-id
  TENANT_ID: your-tenant-id

kubectl apply -f fn-azure-ssl-config.yaml

docs.title: 3. Add the Azure block to values.yaml
docs.text:
Add this to your values.yaml (created in the core guide):

on_aks: true

storage:
  azure:
    secretName: fn-azure-storage
    shareName: files

With TLS auto-renewal:

on_aks: true

storage:
  azure:
    secretName: fn-azure-storage
    shareName: files

cert-manager:
  enabled: true

certs:
  azure:
    configmap: fn-azure-ssl-config
    secretName: fn-azure-ssl-sp

If you are also deploying the Task Controller (outbound mode), use a YAML anchor to avoid duplicating the storage config - the Task Controller needs the same storage secret:

on_aks: true

storage: &storage
  azure:
    secretName: fn-azure-storage
    shareName: files

cert-manager:
  enabled: true

certs:
  azure:
    configmap: fn-azure-ssl-config
    secretName: fn-azure-ssl-sp

fn-task-controller:
  storage: *storage

docs.title: 4. Deploy
docs.text: Return to Deploy: Core step 8 and run helm install with your completed values.yaml.

docs.title: Next step
docs.text: Post-Deploy Testing

docs.title: Deploy: Core
docs.text: This guide covers the steps common to all platforms. Work through this alongside the platform-specific guide for your environment (Azure, AWS, GCP or On-Premises). The platform-specific guides contain additional values to be added to your values.yaml file and additional secrets that must exist before running helm install

docs.title: 1. Add the Helm repository
docs.text:
helm repo add federated-node https://aridhia-open-source.github.io/PHEMS_federated_node
helm repo update

Check available versions:

# Stable releases
helm search repo federated-node --versions

# Include development/pre-release builds
helm search repo federated-node --devel --versions

docs.title: 2. Create a namespace (recommended)
docs.text:
kubectl create namespace federated-node

Append -n federated-node to all kubectl commands in this guide, or omit it if deploying to the default namespace.

docs.title: 3. Create the database credentials secret
docs.text:
The FN needs credentials to connect to your PostgreSQL instance. Store the password in a Kubernetes secret:

kubectl create secret generic fn-db-secret \
    --from-literal=value="<your-db-password>" \
    -n federated-node

Or via YAML (value must be base64-encoded - echo -n "yourpassword" | base64):

apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
metadata:
  name: fn-db-secret
  namespace: federated-node
data:
  value: <base64-encoded-password>
type: Opaque

docs.title: 4. Create the first user secret
docs.text:
From v1.5.0 the chart can create an initial admin user automatically. The password must be stored in a Kubernetes secret - name, passKey, and email are all required if you use firstUserSecret.

kubectl create secret generic fn-first-user \
    --from-literal=password="<your-chosen-password>" \
    -n federated-node

You'll reference this secret by name in values.yaml (step 5). If you skip this, you can retrieve the auto-generated Keycloak admin password from the kc-secrets secret after deployment:

kubectl get secret -n federated-node kc-secrets -o json \
  | jq -r '.data.KEYCLOAK_ADMIN_PASSWORD' | base64 -d

docs.title: 5. Create the TLS secret (if not using cert-manager)
docs.text:
If you already have a certificate:

kubectl create secret tls tls \
    --key key.pem \
    --cert cert.crt \
    -n federated-node

For automatic certificate renewal, see the cert-manager section in your platform-specific guide.

For local development, you can create a self signed certificate using the following example 

HOST=fn.example.com

openssl req -x509 -nodes -days 365 -newkey rsa:2048 \
     -keyout key.pem -out cert.pem \ 
     -subj "/CN=${HOST}/O=${HOST}" -addext "subjectAltName = DNS:${HOST}"

kubectl create secret tls tls \
    --key key.pem \
    --cert cert.crt \
    -n federated-node

docs.title: 6. Pre-install Gateway API and Traefik CRDs (if using Traefik)
docs.text: If traefik.enabled: true, these CRDs must exist before helm install or the chart will fail. See Prerequisites for the install command.

docs.title: 7. Create your values.yaml
docs.text:
Create values.yaml. At minimum you need:

# Public hostname where the FN will be accessible
host: fn.your-institution.example.com

# PostgreSQL connection for FN internal metadata (not your research data)
db:
  host: your-postgres-host.example.com
  name: federated_node_db
  port: 5432
  user: fn_user
  secret:
    name: fn-db-secret   # secret name from step 3
    key: value            # key within that secret

# First admin user (v1.5.0+)
firstUserSecret:
  name: fn-first-user    # secret name from step 4
  passKey: password      # key within that secret holding the password
  email: admin@your-institution.example.com
  firstName: Admin
  lastName: User

# Traefik ingress (recommended for production)
traefik:
  enabled: true

Then add the platform-specific storage block from your platform guide. See the Helm Values Reference for all options.

docs.title: 8. Deploy
docs.text:
helm install federatednode federated-node/federated-node \
    -f values.yaml \
    --namespace federated-node

To deploy into the default namespace, omit --namespace.

To upgrade an existing deployment:

helm upgrade federatednode federated-node/federated-node \
    -f values.yaml \
    --namespace federated-node

Note: the release name is federatednode (no hyphen). Use this exact name for all subsequent helm commands against this release.

docs.title: 9. Check pod status
docs.text:
kubectl get pods -n federated-node
kubectl get pods -n keycloak

All pods should reach Running status. Keycloak and the backend API pods can take 2-3 minutes on first boot. If anything is stuck, check logs:

kubectl logs -n federated-node deployment/backend
kubectl logs -n keycloak statefulset/keycloak

Common causes of failure:

  • Pending - storage PV not provisioned, or insufficient cluster resources
  • CrashLoopBackOff on backend - database unreachable, or db.secret references a non-existent secret
  • CrashLoopBackOff on Keycloak - database unreachable
  • Helm install error about missing CRDs - Gateway API or Traefik CRDs not pre-installed (see step 6)

docs.title: Next step
docs.text: Once your pods are running, go to Post-Deploy Testing to verify everything works end-to-end.

docs.title: Deploy: GCP (GKE)
docs.text:
Work through Deploy: Core alongside this guide. The steps here are the GCP-specific additions to your values.yaml and the IAM setup to do beforehand.

All authentication uses Workload Identity - no service account keys are created or stored.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: The following GKE add-ons must be enabled. Check and enable each if needed.

docs.title: Workload Identity
docs.text:
Workload Identity must be enabled on your GKE cluster. Check first:

gcloud container clusters describe <your-cluster> \
    --region <your-region> \
    --format="value(workloadIdentityConfig.workloadPool)"

If this returns <your-gcp-project>.svc.id.goog, Workload Identity is already enabled. If it returns nothing, enable it:

gcloud container clusters update <your-cluster> \
    --workload-pool=<your-gcp-project>.svc.id.goog \
    --region <your-region>

Workload Identity must also be enabled at the node pool level. Check each node pool:

gcloud container node-pools describe <your-node-pool> \
    --cluster <your-cluster> \
    --region <your-region> \
    --format="value(config.workloadMetadataConfig.mode)"

If this returns GKE_METADATA, it is already enabled. If not:

gcloud container node-pools update <your-node-pool> \
    --cluster <your-cluster> \
    --region <your-region> \
    --workload-metadata=GKE_METADATA

docs.title: GCS FUSE CSI driver
docs.text:
Required for mounting GCS buckets as volumes. Check first:

gcloud container clusters describe <your-cluster> \
    --region <your-region> \
    --format="value(addonsConfig.gcsFuseCsiDriverConfig.enabled)"

If this returns nothing or false, enable it:

gcloud container clusters update <your-cluster> \
    --region <your-region> \
    --update-addons GcsFuseCsiDriver=ENABLED

Both updates take several minutes to roll out across the node pool.

docs.title: 1. Storage
docs.text:
The FN uses GCS FUSE as the ReadWriteMany storage backend, mounting a Google Cloud Storage bucket directly into pods.

The GCS bucket must already exist before deploying.

docs.title: 1a. Create a service account and grant bucket access
docs.text:
gcloud iam service-accounts create fn-storage \
    --display-name "FN Storage"

gcloud storage buckets add-iam-policy-binding gs://<your-bucket> \
    --member "serviceAccount:fn-storage@<your-gcp-project>.iam.gserviceaccount.com" \
    --role "roles/storage.objectAdmin"

docs.title: 1b. Bind Workload Identity
docs.text:
The FN backend runs as the secret-backend-handler Kubernetes service account in the release namespace. Task pods run as default in the tasks namespace. Both need access to the bucket:

# Backend pods
gcloud iam service-accounts add-iam-policy-binding \
    fn-storage@<your-gcp-project>.iam.gserviceaccount.com \
    --role roles/iam.workloadIdentityUser \
    --member "serviceAccount:<your-gcp-project>.svc.id.goog[federated-node/secret-backend-handler]"

# Task pods
gcloud iam service-accounts add-iam-policy-binding \
    fn-storage@<your-gcp-project>.iam.gserviceaccount.com \
    --role roles/iam.workloadIdentityUser \
    --member "serviceAccount:<your-gcp-project>.svc.id.goog[tasks/default]"

# Task controller pod (if deploying in outbound mode)
gcloud iam service-accounts add-iam-policy-binding \
    fn-storage@<your-gcp-project>.iam.gserviceaccount.com \
    --role roles/iam.workloadIdentityUser \
    --member "serviceAccount:<your-gcp-project>.svc.id.goog[fn-controller/analytics-operator]"

Replace federated-node, tasks, and fn-controller with the namespaces you are deploying to if different from the defaults.

docs.title: 2. TLS auto-renewal (optional)
docs.text: Automatic SSL certificate renewal uses cert-manager with GCP Cloud DNS for the DNS-01 challenge.

docs.title: 2a. Create a service account and grant DNS access
docs.text:
gcloud iam service-accounts create cert-manager-dns \
    --display-name "cert-manager Cloud DNS"

gcloud projects add-iam-policy-binding <your-gcp-project> \
    --member "serviceAccount:cert-manager-dns@<your-gcp-project>.iam.gserviceaccount.com" \
    --role "roles/dns.admin"

docs.title: 2b. Bind Workload Identity
docs.text:
gcloud iam service-accounts add-iam-policy-binding \
    cert-manager-dns@<your-gcp-project>.iam.gserviceaccount.com \
    --role roles/iam.workloadIdentityUser \
    --member "serviceAccount:<your-gcp-project>.svc.id.goog[fn-certmanager/<release-name>-cert-manager]"

[fn-certmanager/<release-name>-cert-manager] is [<cert-manager-namespace>/<release-name>-cert-manager]. The cert-manager Helm subchart prefixes the Helm release name to its service account - if you installed with helm install federatednode ..., the KSA is federatednode-cert-manager. The default cert-manager namespace in this chart is fn-certmanager.

To confirm the exact KSA name after installing: kubectl get serviceaccounts -n fn-certmanager

docs.title: 2c. Annotate the cert-manager service account
docs.text:
Add this to your values.yaml so Helm passes it to the cert-manager subchart:

cert-manager:
  serviceAccount:
    annotations:
      iam.gke.io/gcp-service-account: cert-manager-dns@<your-gcp-project>.iam.gserviceaccount.com

docs.title: 3. Add the GCP block to values.yaml
docs.text:
Add this to your values.yaml (created in the core guide):

on_gke: true

storage:
  gcp:
    bucketName: <your-bucket>

With TLS auto-renewal:

on_gke: true

storage:
  gcp:
    bucketName: <your-bucket>

cert-manager:
  enabled: true
  serviceAccount:
    annotations:
      iam.gke.io/gcp-service-account: cert-manager-dns@<your-gcp-project>.iam.gserviceaccount.com

certs:
  gcp:
    email: admin@your-institution.example.com
    project: <your-gcp-project>

If you are also deploying the Task Controller (outbound mode), use a YAML anchor to avoid duplicating the storage config:

on_gke: true

storage: &storage
  gcp:
    bucketName: <your-bucket>

cert-manager:
  enabled: true
  serviceAccount:
    annotations:
      iam.gke.io/gcp-service-account: cert-manager-dns@<your-gcp-project>.iam.gserviceaccount.com

certs:
  gcp:
    email: admin@your-institution.example.com
    project: <your-gcp-project>

fn-task-controller:
  storage: *storage

docs.title: 4. Deploy
docs.text: Return to Deploy: Core step 8 and run helm install with your completed values.yaml.

docs.title: 5. Annotate the Kubernetes service accounts
docs.text:
The Kubernetes service accounts and namespaces are created by Helm, so this must be done after helm install. Annotate first, then restart the pods to pick up the new Workload Identity:

kubectl annotate serviceaccount secret-backend-handler \
    --namespace federated-node \
    iam.gke.io/gcp-service-account=fn-storage@<your-gcp-project>.iam.gserviceaccount.com

kubectl annotate serviceaccount default \
    --namespace tasks \
    iam.gke.io/gcp-service-account=fn-storage@<your-gcp-project>.iam.gserviceaccount.com

# Task controller (if deploying in outbound mode)
kubectl annotate serviceaccount analytics-operator \
    --namespace fn-controller \
    iam.gke.io/gcp-service-account=fn-storage@<your-gcp-project>.iam.gserviceaccount.com

# Restart pods to pick up the new identity
kubectl rollout restart deployment/backend --namespace federated-node
kubectl rollout restart deployment/analytics-operator --namespace fn-controller

docs.title: Deploy: On-Premises
docs.text:
Work through Deploy: Core alongside this guide.

This guide covers production on-premises deployments using distributions commonly used in healthcare and enterprise environments. Local single-node setups (e.g. for development) are covered briefly at the end.

docs.title: Choosing a distribution
docs.text:
The FN has been tested on RKE2 and that is the recommended distribution for on-premises deployments. It is hardened by default (CIS benchmark), uses containerd, and is well suited to healthcare and regulated environments.

Other CNCF-conformant distributions - including k3s and kubeadm - should work given the FN has no hard dependency on any specific distribution, but these have not been formally tested. The steps in this guide are written for RKE2 and note where behaviour may differ on other distributions.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text: Complete Prerequisites, including the Gateway API and Traefik CRD pre-install step - this is required before helm install if you are using Traefik as your ingress.

docs.title: Storage
docs.text: The FN requires a ReadWriteMany persistent volume for task results. The chart creates its own StorageClass (federatednode-shared-results) and PersistentVolume. You configure which backend that volume uses.

docs.title: NFS (recommended for multi-node production clusters)
docs.text:
NFS is the most practical ReadWriteMany solution for on-premises multi-node clusters. Any node in the cluster can read and write results without pod scheduling constraints.

Prerequisites:

  • An NFS server accessible from all cluster nodes (a dedicated NAS, a standalone Linux host, or existing storage infrastructure)

Ensure the export directory on your NFS server is writable by the FN pods, which run as non-root UID 1000:

mkdir -p /exports/federated-node
chown 1000:1000 /exports/federated-node
chmod 775 /exports/federated-node

Add to values.yaml:

storage:
  capacity: 50Gi
  nfs:
    url: 192.168.1.100            # your NFS server IP or hostname
    path: /exports/federated-node # exported path on the NFS server

Optional: If you have csi-driver-nfs installed, you can set storage.nfs.provisioner: nfs.csi.k8s.io to use it as the StorageClass provisioner label. It is not required - the NFS mount works without it.

docs.title: Local host path (single-node or development only)
docs.text:
Local path storage pins task pods to the node that holds the data. This is fine for single-node clusters or development, but not suitable for multi-node production - if the pod is scheduled on a different node it won't find its volume.

Create the directory, ensuring the FN's non-root user (UID 1000) can write to it:

mkdir -p /data/federated-node/results
chown 1000:1000 /data/federated-node/results

Add to values.yaml:

storage:
  capacity: 50Gi
  local:
    path: /data/federated-node/results

docs.title: Ingress
docs.text: The FN uses Traefik with the Kubernetes Gateway API. The chart bundles Traefik as a subchart - you do not need to install it separately, and you do not need to remove or disable any existing ingress controller on your cluster.

docs.title: Coexistence with existing ingress controllers
docs.text:
RKE2 and k3s both ship with their own bundled Traefik instance. The FN's Traefik can run alongside it without conflict. The two instances are isolated by design:

  • RKE2/k3s's Traefik registers as IngressClass traefik and watches standard Ingress resources
  • The FN's Traefik registers its own GatewayClass (traefik-fn-gateway-class) and only watches Gateway and HTTPRoute resources that reference that class

They route completely independently and neither will interfere with the other's traffic.

The one practical consideration is port exposure: if your existing ingress controller already claims port 443 on all nodes, you need to expose the FN's Traefik on a different address - either via a separate IP (MetalLB pool, floating IP), a different NodePort, or behind your existing load balancer as a named virtual host. See the Exposing Traefik section below.

docs.title: kubeadm
docs.text: No bundled ingress. Install the Gateway API and Traefik CRDs (see Prerequisites) and set traefik.enabled: true in your values.

docs.title: Exposing Traefik to your network
docs.text: Traefik listens internally on port 8443 (HTTPS) and 8000 (HTTP). You need to make port 443 accessible to users. The right approach depends on your infrastructure.

docs.title: Using a hardware or software load balancer (recommended)
docs.text:
If your environment has an existing load balancer (F5, HAProxy, nginx, MetalLB), configure it to forward port 443 to the Traefik service's NodePort or ClusterIP.

MetalLB is a common choice for on-premises Kubernetes - it gives Traefik a real external IP from your network's address range without needing cloud infrastructure. Follow the MetalLB installation guide to set it up, then once Traefik has claimed an IP, add that to your DNS for the host value in your FN values.

If you want to lock Traefik to a specific IP rather than letting MetalLB assign one, set it explicitly:

traefik:
  enabled: true
  service:
    spec:
      externalIPs:
        - 192.168.1.200

docs.title: Using NodePort with an external reverse proxy
docs.text:
If you cannot run MetalLB, expose Traefik as a NodePort and point an existing reverse proxy (nginx, HAProxy) at it:

traefik:
  enabled: true
  service:
    type: NodePort

Then configure your reverse proxy to forward 443 -> <any-node-ip>:<traefik-nodeport>.

docs.title: With cert-manager (recommended if you have a public or ACME-compatible CA)
docs.text:
cert-manager automates certificate renewal. Install it via the FN chart itself:

cert-manager:
  enabled: true
  installCRDs: true

For internal CA or Let's Encrypt with DNS-01 challenge, configure a ClusterIssuer after deployment. The FN chart's built-in issuer uses Let's Encrypt with DNS-01 (Azure or AWS DNS). For other DNS providers, install cert-manager separately and manage the ClusterIssuer manually, pointing it at your CA.

docs.title: With an existing certificate
docs.text:
If your institution has a PKI or provides certificates from an internal CA:

kubectl create secret tls tls \
    --key server.key \
    --cert server.crt \
    -n federated-node

Reference it in values:

tls:
  secretName: tls

The certificate's CN or SAN must match your host value. Intermediate certificates should be bundled into server.crt (full chain).

docs.title: Self-signed (internal/development only)
docs.text:
openssl req -x509 -nodes -days 365 -newkey rsa:2048 \
  -keyout server.key \
  -out server.crt \
  -subj "/CN=fn.your-institution.internal"

kubectl create secret tls tls \
    --key server.key \
    --cert server.crt \
    -n federated-node

Clients will need to trust your CA or accept the self-signed cert.

docs.title: PostgreSQL
docs.text:
Provide an external PostgreSQL instance. Options commonly used on-prem:

  • CloudNativePG or Zalando Postgres Operator - run a managed PostgreSQL cluster inside Kubernetes
  • Standalone PostgreSQL on a VM or bare-metal host outside the cluster
  • Patroni - for HA PostgreSQL

The FN does not need a dedicated server - a shared PostgreSQL instance with a dedicated database and user is sufficient. The FN creates its own schema on first boot.

Minimum: PostgreSQL 12, 1 vCPU, 2 GB RAM for the FN's own metadata database.

docs.title: Pod security
docs.text:
The FN pods run non-root (runAsNonRoot: true, UID 1000) with allowPrivilegeEscalation: false, all Linux capabilities dropped, and seccompProfile: RuntimeDefault. This is compatible with:

  • RKE2's default Pod Security Standards (restricted or baseline namespace labels)
  • CIS-hardened cluster profiles

If your cluster enforces restricted Pod Security Standards, label the FN namespaces accordingly:

kubectl label namespace federated-node \
  pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=restricted

kubectl label namespace keycloak \
  pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=restricted

kubectl label namespace tasks \
  pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=baseline

The tasks namespace runs analytics containers whose security posture depends on the images your researchers provide - use baseline there unless you control all analytics images.

The chart also creates a ClusterRole giving the backend service account broad permissions over pods, PVs, PVCs, jobs, and secrets (needed to dynamically create per-task storage and run task pods). This is expected behaviour - ensure your cluster's RBAC policies permit ClusterRole creation by the deploying user.

docs.title: Complete values.yaml example (RKE2, NFS, MetalLB)
docs.text:
host: fn.your-institution.internal

db:
  host: postgres.db.svc.cluster.local   # or external PostgreSQL host
  name: federated_node_db
  port: 5432
  user: fn_user
  secret:
    name: fn-db-secret
    key: value

firstUserSecret:
  name: fn-first-user
  passKey: password
  email: admin@your-institution.example.com
  firstName: Admin
  lastName: User

storage:
  capacity: 50Gi
  nfs:
    provisioner: nfs-client
    url: 192.168.1.100
    path: /exports/federated-node

traefik:
  enabled: true
  service:
    spec:
      externalIPs:
        - 192.168.1.200   # MetalLB or static IP

tls:
  secretName: tls   # pre-created TLS secret

keycloak:
  replicas: 2

cleanupTime: 7

integrations:
  domains:
    - https://fn.your-institution.internal

docs.title: Networking checklist
docs.text:
Before deploying, confirm:

  • [ ] Cluster nodes can reach your PostgreSQL host on port 5432
  • [ ] Cluster nodes can reach your NFS server on the NFS port (2049)
  • [ ] Cluster nodes can reach container registries (ghcr.io, and wherever your analytics images are hosted)
  • [ ] The Traefik external IP or NodePort is reachable from researcher workstations
  • [ ] If using the Task Controller: cluster nodes have outbound HTTPS access to github.com
  • [ ] If using cert-manager with DNS-01: cluster nodes can reach your DNS provider's API

docs.title: Helm Values Reference
docs.text:
Complete reference for all configuration fields in the Federated Node Helm chart values.yaml.

All fields are optional unless marked required.

docs.title: General
docs.text: Field Description Default host Public URL where the FN will be hosted. Also used to name result files. - cleanupTime Days to retain task results and related Kubernetes resources. Cleanup runs daily at noon via a CronJob. 3 taskReview Enable the results review/approval workflow (see Task Review) false outboundMode Deploy the Federated Node Task Controller as a subchart false smoketests Enable smoke test endpoints for helm test false on_aks Set to true when deploying on Azure AKS false on_eks Set to true when deploying on AWS EKS false pullPolicy Image pull policy for all FN images. Options: Always, IfNotPresent Always

docs.title: Backend
docs.text: Field Description Default backend.replicas Number of backend pod replicas 1 backend.tag Override the backend image tag (for testing specific versions) Chart appVersion federatedNode.port Backend service port 5000 federatedNode.volumes.results_path Mount path for results storage inside the backend pod /mnt/results federatedNode.volumes.task_pod_results_path Mount path for results storage inside analytics task pods /mnt/data federatedNode.enable_image_whitelist Restrict task execution to images on the allowlist. When false, any image from a registered registry is permitted. false federatedNode.allow_delivery_api Automatically deliver results when a task completes via direct API call (not just Task Controller triggers) false

docs.title: Keycloak
docs.text: Field Description Default keycloak.replicas Number of Keycloak pod replicas 2 keycloak.tag Override the Keycloak image tag Chart appVersion

docs.title: Database (required)
docs.text:
The fields db.host, db.user, and db.secret are required.

Field Description Default db.host Required. PostgreSQL hostname - db.user Required. Database username - db.secret.name Required. Kubernetes secret containing the password - db.secret.key Required. Key within the secret where the password is stored - db.name Database name fndb db.port Database port 5432 db.enforceSSL Enforce SSL on the FN backend's connection to PostgreSQL false

docs.title: First user (v1.5.0+)
docs.text:
If firstUserSecret is provided, name, passKey, and email are all required. The secret holding the password must exist in the same namespace before deploying.

Field Description Default firstUserSecret.name Required if using firstUserSecret. Kubernetes secret name containing the password - firstUserSecret.passKey Required if using firstUserSecret. Key within the secret holding the password - firstUserSecret.email Required if using firstUserSecret. User's email address (also used as the login username) - firstUserSecret.firstName User's first name (optional) - firstUserSecret.lastName User's last name (optional) -

If firstUserSecret is omitted, retrieve the auto-generated Keycloak admin password post-deploy: 

kubectl get secret -n <namespace> kc-secrets -o json | jq -r '.data.KEYCLOAK_ADMIN_PASSWORD' | base64 -d

docs.title: Storage
docs.text:
Exactly one of azure, aws, nfs, or local must be provided.

Field Description Default storage.capacity Persistent volume size for task results 10Gi storage.mountOptions List of mount options passed to the storage volume [] storage.azure.secretName Kubernetes secret with Azure Storage Account credentials - storage.azure.shareName Azure file share name - storage.azure.provisioner Override the Azure storage class provisioner disk.csi.azure.com storage.aws.fileSystemId Required for AWS. EFS filesystem ID (e.g. fs-xxxxxxxxx) - storage.aws.accessPointId Required for AWS. EFS access point ID - storage.nfs.provisioner NFS storage class provisioner name - storage.nfs.url NFS server hostname or IP - storage.nfs.path Path on the NFS server - storage.local.path Host path for results storage (local/on-prem only) - storage.local.dbpath Host path for DB storage - only used when create_db_deployment: true -

docs.title: Dataset volumes
docs.text:
Read-only volumes holding DuckDB/SQLite files for file datasets. Each entry creates a ReadOnlyMany PV, and a PVC named name in the tasks namespace to use as the dataset's volume_claim. Set exactly one of local, azure, aws, gcp or nfs per entry.

Field Description Default datasetVolumes[].name PVC name, referenced by the dataset's volume_claim - datasetVolumes[].capacity Volume size 10Gi datasetVolumes[].mountOptions List of mount options [] datasetVolumes[].local.path Directory on the node - datasetVolumes[].azure.shareName Azure file share name - datasetVolumes[].azure.secretName Secret with the storage account credentials azure-storage-secret datasetVolumes[].azure.secretNamespace Namespace of that secret - datasetVolumes[].aws.fileSystemId EFS filesystem ID - datasetVolumes[].aws.accessPointId EFS access point ID (optional) - datasetVolumes[].gcp.bucketName GCS bucket, mounted via GCS FUSE - datasetVolumes[].nfs.url NFS server hostname or IP - datasetVolumes[].nfs.path Path on the NFS server -
